paras: The killing of Barfield took place in Miller County, Georgia, shortly before July 2, 1888; the papers gave neither his first name nor his race. His widow, Elizabeth Barfield, wrote to a federal deputy marshal that he had been "murdered by the kuklux," while another report said a deputy sheriff had killed him as he resisted arrest.

On July 2, 1888, Elizabeth Barfield wrote from Miller County to the deputy United States marshal at Albany asking for protection. She wrote that her husband had been murdered by the "kuklux," that they had threatened the life of her son, who was about 15, and that she could prove who they were. Describing her home as in Miller County "south west of Minis' mill, in Baker county," she asked the marshal to come at once to protect her house. The marshal received the letter on Tuesday, July 3.

Around the same time, a band of Miller County "regulators" posted a notice on a plantation in Baker County warning all hands to leave under penalty of death. According to the Constitution, the proprietors armed the laborers with rifles, and the laborers stayed.

Against the widow's signed charge, the papers set an unattributed statement, made when news of the killing first arrived, that a deputy sheriff had killed him while he resisted arrest. Neither paper named the deputy, gave a charge against Barfield, or named the men the widow said she could identify.
No report of an inquest, arrest or action by the marshal appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News printed the letter on July 5 among state paragraphs in its "Georgia and Florida" column, without comment; its text breaks off after "warning all hands to leave." Five days later the Atlanta Constitution ran nearly the same text in its weekly "Through Dixie" roundup, completing the sentence about the regulators and giving the item a subhead, "A Letter from a Woman Which Creates a Sensation." Neither paper chose between the Klan charge and the deputy-sheriff version or identified the race of anyone involved.

reader.title: Killing of Barfield in Miller County, Georgia
bases: The widow's letter says her husband was 'murdered by the kuklux', an alleged killing by an organized band, though an unattributed report said a deputy sheriff killed him resisting arrest (A2, A3).

Barfield was killed (A2, A3), but the widow's 'kuklux' charge and the report of a deputy sheriff killing him while resisting arrest conflict, no number of attackers is given, and no motive or accusation is stated, so the coverage cannot establish an illegal killing by three or more under a pretext of justice or tradition.

The two reports print the same letter and paragraph (A2, A3), so they rest on one source, and within it the widow's account of a Klan murder is contradicted by the report that a deputy sheriff killed Barfield while resisting arrest.
